'''Lydia Phindile Makhubu''' (1 July 1937 - July 2021) was a [[Eswatini|Swazi]] [[chemist]] and former professor of chemistry, [[dean (education)|dean]] and [[vice-chancellor]] of the University of Swaziland (now the [[University of Eswatini]]).<ref name="Yount">{{cite book|last=Yount|first=Lisa|title=A to Z of Women in Science and Math|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=428i2UdWRRAC&pg=PA187|access-date=24 October 2016|year=2007|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=9781438107950|pages=187–188}}{{unreliable source?|date=May 2018}}</ref>

==Life==
She was born at the [[Usuthu Mission]] in Swaziland. Her parents were teachers, but her father also worked as an [[orderly]] in health clinics. Her early exposure to medicine had a great influence on her choice of career; she initially wanted to become a doctor, but then switched to chemistry.<ref name="CR">{{cite book |title=Biology |last1=Campbell |first1=Neil A. |last2=Reece |first2=Jane B. |edition=7th |url=http://wps.aw.com/bc_campbell_biology_10_oa/244/62525/16006418.cw/index.html |access-date=2016-10-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170930124012/http://wps.aw.com/bc_campbell_biology_10_oa/244/62525/16006418.cw/index.html |archive-date=2017-09-30 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Makhubu graduated from Pius XII College (now the [[National University of Lesotho]]) in [[Lesotho]] with a B.Sc. in 1963. With a Canadian [[Commonwealth scholarship]], she obtained an M.Sc. in [[organic chemistry]] from the [[University of Alberta]] in 1967, followed by a Ph.D. in [[medicinal chemistry]] from the [[University of Toronto]] in 1973,<ref name="SMU">{{cite web |url=https://www.smu.ca/academics/archives/lydia-p-makhubu.html |title=Lydia P. Makhubu |publisher=Saint Mary's University}}</ref> becoming the first Swazi woman to earn a doctorate.<ref name="Yount"/>

She returned to her homeland and joined the faculty of the University of Swaziland, becoming a [[lecturer]] in the chemistry department in 1973, the dean of science from 1976 to 1980, a senior lecturer in 1979, a full [[professor]] the following year, and vice-chancellor from 1988 to 2003.<ref name="Yount"/> Her research focused on the medical effects of plants used by traditional Swazi healers.<ref name="Yount"/><ref name="CR"/>

From its inception in 1993 until 2005, Makhubu was the President of the [[Third World Organization for Women in Science]], which provides fellowships for postgraduate study.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.nature.com/wcs/1news/29-1c.html|title=Nature World Conference on Science|date=29 June 1999|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|access-date=25 November 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.hinduonnet.com/2000/10/19/stories/0219000c.htm|title='Women must be encouraged to take up science'|date=19 October 2007|newspaper=[[The Hindu]]|access-date=25 November 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050224031959/http://www.hinduonnet.com/2000/10/19/stories/0219000c.htm|archive-date=24 February 2005|url-status=usurped}}</ref> She was the first woman chairperson of the executive committee of the [[Association of Commonwealth Universities]].<ref name="SMU"/> She also served in numerous other organizations, such as the United Nations Advisory Committee on Science and Technology for Development.<ref name="SMU"/>

She received numerous grants and honours, including a [[MacArthur Foundation]] grant (1993–1995),<ref name="Oakes">{{cite book|last=Oakes|first=Elizabeth H.|title=Encyclopedia of World Scientists|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&pg=PA478|year=2007|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=9781438118826|pages=477–478}}</ref> and honorary doctorates from various universities,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://archive.unu.edu/news/unu-gdn/unu-gdn-makhubu.htm |title=Curriculum Vitae |publisher=[[United Nations University]] |date=2000}}</ref> including a doctor of laws from [[Saint Mary's University (Halifax)|Saint Mary's University]] in 1991.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.smu.ca/academics/archives/honorary-degrees.html |title=Honorary Degrees 1990 - Present |publisher=St. Mary's University}}</ref>

She married the surgeon [[Daniel Mbatha]]; they have a son and a daughter.<ref name="Yount"/>
